title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media. A video call presented a generated likeness of a sitting chief minister, and the likeness was the whole of the credential, since a WhatsApp call carries no way for the person receiving it to confirm who is on the other end. The fraud did not depend on breaking any system. It depended on the victim treating an unverifiable channel as an authoritative one.

The failure sits at the point of first contact, and it was compounded by a second claimed identity, a person presenting himself as a CBI officer, which converted a promise of aid into a threat of penalty. Catching it would have required verification outside the call itself, through an official office or channel that the caller does not control. The requests for advance payments to release money are the part of the sequence that a check could have interrupted, because no legitimate disbursement of aid requires the recipient to pay fees first.

What is not established is who produced the deepfake or operated the scheme. The account comes from a single outlet, a police case was registered under the Information Technology Act, and a registered case is not a finding of guilt against any person.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29 year old security guard in Bengaluru, Ratikanta Giri, who is from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on September 9. The caller appeared as an AI generated deepfake of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and promised Rs 11 lakh in financial aid. A supposed manager said Rs 5 lakh had been allotted and asked Giri to pay fees. Giri paid Rs 5,000 as exchange charges and Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN.

A person claiming to be CBI officer Thakur then demanded more than Rs 50,000 as a fine. Fearing he would lose earlier payments, Giri paid and made further transfers totaling over Rs 1.04 lakh. When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he had been duped. He contacted cybercrime helpline 1930 and Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act. Police urged people not to believe such calls or make payments based on them.
